Content:
The negation of a mathematical statement is its opposite statement. A mathematical statement and its negation have opposite truth values.

Content:
For example:

Content:
- The negation of the true statement "[MATH: 4] is divisible by [MATH: 2]" is the false statement "[MATH: 4] is not divisible by [MATH: 2.]"
- The negation of the false statement "[MATH: 5] is even" is the true statement "[MATH: 5] is odd."

Content:
We can express negations using the symbol "[MATH: \neg]". The negation of [MATH: A] is denoted [MATH: \neg A,] and has the opposite truth values as [MATH: A{:}]

We can negate compound statements as well. For example, the statement [MATH: \neg (A \land B)] has the opposite truth values as the statement [MATH: A \land B{:}]

items.title: Negating a Plain English Statement

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the following statement.

[MATH: P: 1] is not smaller than [MATH: 2]

Which of following represents [MATH: \neg P?]
sections.readable_text:
Consider the following statement.

> [MATH: P: 1] is not smaller than [MATH: 2]

Which of following represents [MATH: \neg P?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The symbol "[MATH: eg]" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence.

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

It is not true that [MATH: 1] is not smaller than [MATH: 2.]

In other words, [MATH: 1] is smaller than [MATH: 2.] Therefore, [MATH: eg P] means the following:

[MATH: 1] is smaller than [MATH: 2.]

Note that [MATH: P] is false, while [MATH: eg P] is true.
sections.readable_text:
The symbol "[MATH: \neg]" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence.

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

> It is not true that [MATH: 1] is not smaller than [MATH: 2.]

In other words, [MATH: 1] is smaller than [MATH: 2.] Therefore, [MATH: \neg P] means the following:

> [MATH: 1] is smaller than [MATH: 2.]

Note that [MATH: P] is false, while [MATH: \neg P] is true.

items.title: Expressing a Negated Sentence in Symbolic Form

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the following statement:

[MATH: \dfrac12] is not a natural number, or [MATH: \sqrt{2}] is not a real number.

Express the compound statement above in symbolic form given the following:

  • [MATH: (1)/(2)]

  • [MATH: sqrt(2)]
sections.readable_text:
Consider the following statement:

> [MATH: \dfrac12] is not a natural number, or [MATH: \sqrt{2}] is not a real number.

Express the compound statement above in symbolic form given the following:

- [MATH: (1)/(2)]
- [MATH: sqrt(2)]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The sentence

[MATH: \dfrac12] is not a natural number

can be expressed symbolically as [MATH: eg P.]

The sentence

[MATH: \sqrt{2}] is not a real number

can be expressed symbolically as [MATH: eg Q.]

Therefore, the sentence

[MATH: \dfrac12] is not a natural number, or [MATH: \sqrt{2}] is not a real number

can be expressed symbolically as [MATH: eg P \lor eg Q.]
sections.readable_text:
The sentence

> [MATH: \dfrac12] is not a natural number

can be expressed symbolically as [MATH: \neg P.]

The sentence

> [MATH: \sqrt{2}] is not a real number

can be expressed symbolically as [MATH: \neg Q.]

Therefore, the sentence

> [MATH: \dfrac12] is not a natural number, or [MATH: \sqrt{2}] is not a real number

can be expressed symbolically as [MATH: \neg P \lor \neg Q.]

Content:
When we have two negations in a row, we can cancel them out.

Content:
- For example, [MATH: \neg (\neg A)] can be simplified to [MATH: A.]

Content:
To understand why negations cancel with each other, consider the following statement:

Content:
> [MATH: 4] is divisible by [MATH: 2.]

Content:
The negation of this statement is

Content:
> [MATH: 4] is not divisible by [MATH: 2.]

Content:
If we negate again, we get back the original sentence:

Content:
> [MATH: 4] divisible by [MATH: 2.]

Content:
So, if we negate a statement twice, we end up with the original statement.

Content:
More formally, we can prove that [MATH: \neg (\neg A) \equiv A] using a truth table.

Content:
| [MATH: \,A\,] | [MATH: \,\neg A\,] | [MATH: \,\neg(\neg A)\,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |

Content:
Since [MATH: A] and [MATH: \neg(\neg A)] have the same truth values, they are logically equivalent.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The negation of a mathematical statement is its opposite statement. A mathematical statement and its negation have opposite truth values.

Content:
For example:

Content:
- The negation of the true statement "[MATH: 4] is divisible by [MATH: 2]" is the false statement "[MATH: 4] is not divisible by [MATH: 2.]"
- The negation of the false statement "[MATH: 5] is even" is the true statement "[MATH: 5] is odd."

Content:
We can express negations using the symbol "[MATH: \neg]". The negation of [MATH: A] is denoted [MATH: \neg A,] and has the opposite truth values as [MATH: A{:}]

Content:
| [MATH: \,A\,] | [MATH: \,\neg A\,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |

Content:
We can negate compound statements as well. For example, the statement [MATH: \neg (A \land B)] has the opposite truth values as the statement [MATH: A \land B{:}]

Content:
| [MATH: \,A\,] | [MATH: \,B\,] | [MATH: \, A \land B \,] | [MATH: \, \neg (A \land B) \,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |

---

Item 2 — Example: Negating a Plain English Statement

Example Prompt:
Consider the following statement.

> [MATH: P: 1] is not smaller than [MATH: 2]

Which of following represents [MATH: \neg P?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The symbol "[MATH: \neg]" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence.

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

> It is not true that [MATH: 1] is not smaller than [MATH: 2.]

In other words, [MATH: 1] is smaller than [MATH: 2.] Therefore, [MATH: \neg P] means the following:

> [MATH: 1] is smaller than [MATH: 2.]

Note that [MATH: P] is false, while [MATH: \neg P] is true.

---

Item 5 — Example: Expressing a Negated Sentence in Symbolic Form

Example Prompt:
Consider the following statement:

> [MATH: \dfrac12] is not a natural number, or [MATH: \sqrt{2}] is not a real number.

Express the compound statement above in symbolic form given the following:

- [MATH: (1)/(2)]
- [MATH: sqrt(2)]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The sentence

> [MATH: \dfrac12] is not a natural number

can be expressed symbolically as [MATH: \neg P.]

The sentence

> [MATH: \sqrt{2}] is not a real number

can be expressed symbolically as [MATH: \neg Q.]

Therefore, the sentence

> [MATH: \dfrac12] is not a natural number, or [MATH: \sqrt{2}] is not a real number

can be expressed symbolically as [MATH: \neg P \lor \neg Q.]

Item 8 — Example: Completing a Truth Table for a Compound Statement

Example Prompt:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| [MATH: \,P\,] | [MATH: \,Q\,] | [MATH: \, \neg (P \land \neg Q)\,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\phantom{F}}] |

| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\phantom{F}}] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\phantom{F}}] |

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we add a column for [MATH: \neg Q.] Remember that the truth values of [MATH: \neg Q] are opposite those of [MATH: Q.]

| [MATH: \,P\,] | [MATH: \,Q\,] | [MATH: \, \neg Q\,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |

Then, we add a column for [MATH: P \land \neg Q.] Remember that [MATH: P \land \neg Q] is true if both [MATH: P] and [MATH: \neg Q] are true.

| [MATH: \,P\,] | [MATH: \,Q\,] | [MATH: \, \neg Q\,] | [MATH: \, P \land \neg Q\,] |

| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |

Finally, we add a column for [MATH: \neg ( P \land \neg Q ).] Remember that the truth values of [MATH: \neg (P \land \neg Q)] are opposite those of [MATH: P \land \neg Q.]

| [MATH: \,P\,] | [MATH: \,Q\,] | [MATH: \, \neg Q\,] | [MATH: \, P \land \neg Q\,] | [MATH: \, \neg (P \land \neg Q) \,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}] |

Item 11 — Tutorial: Double Negations

Content:
When we have two negations in a row, we can cancel them out.

Content:
- For example, [MATH: \neg (\neg A)] can be simplified to [MATH: A.]
- Likewise, [MATH: \neg (\neg (A \land B))] can be simplified to [MATH: A \land B.]

Content:

Content:

Content:

Content:
So, if we negate a statement twice, we end up with the original statement.

Content:
More formally, we can prove that [MATH: \neg (\neg A) \equiv A] using a truth table.

Content:
| [MATH: \,A\,] | [MATH: \,\neg A\,] | [MATH: \,\neg(\neg A)\,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |

Since [MATH: A] and [MATH: \neg(\neg A)] have the same truth values, they are logically equivalent.
